solution:
Osmotic pressure is the hydrostatic pressure that has to build up on the solution side to STOP osmosis, that is, to stop the net flow of solvent into the solution through a semipermeable membrane.

For a dilute solution it is given by

\(\pi = MRT\)

where \(M\) is the molarity of the solution, \(R\) the gas constant and \(T\) the temperature.

The chapter adds an important caution: osmotic pressure is NOT a pressure produced by the solution by itself. It exists only when the solution is separated from the pure solvent by a suitable semipermeable membrane.

Because osmotic pressure is measured at one fixed temperature.

Molarity (moles of solute per \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of SOLUTION) changes with temperature, since the volume of the solution expands or contracts on heating. Molality (moles of solute per kg of SOLVENT) is a ratio of two masses and is therefore temperature independent.

A temperature-independent unit is needed only when the temperature changes during the measurement, as it does for boiling point elevation and freezing point depression. An osmotic pressure measurement is made at a specific constant temperature, so that precaution is unnecessary and the equation \(\pi = MRT\) is written directly in molarity.

The boiling point elevation is directly proportional to the molality of the solution:

\(\Delta T_b \propto m\) or \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\)

where \(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\) is the boiling point elevation, \(m\) is the molality of the solution and \(K_b\) is the boiling point elevation constant (molal elevation constant or ebullioscopic constant), with units \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).

Writing the molality in terms of the masses, \(m = \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\), the same relation becomes

\(\Delta T_b = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

[Textbook misprint: the printed freezing point \(-4.3^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(i = 4.3/(1.86 \times 0.1) = 23.1\), which is impossible, since \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) yields at most 3 particles per formula unit. A freezing point of \(-0.43^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives the admissible \(i = 2.31\), so the decimal point appears to be misplaced. The question is worked below exactly as printed.]

The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the observed freezing point depression to the value expected for a nonelectrolyte of the same concentration:

\(i = \dfrac{(\Delta T_f)}{(\Delta T_f)_0} = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_f m}\)

Working with the data exactly as printed:

\(\Delta T_f = 0^\circ\mathrm{C} - (-4.3^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 4.3\ \mathrm{K}\)

\((\Delta T_f)_0 = K_f m = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}} = 0.186\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(i = \dfrac{4.3\ \mathrm{K}}{0.186\ \mathrm{K}} = 23.1\)

This value is not physically possible. \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) dissociates as \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{K^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\), giving at most 3 particles per formula unit, so \(i\) cannot exceed 3. A freezing point of \(-0.43^\circ\mathrm{C}\) would give

\(i = \dfrac{0.43\ \mathrm{K}}{0.186\ \mathrm{K}} = 2.31\)

which is an admissible value (below the ideal 3, as expected once ion pairing is allowed for). The printed freezing point therefore appears to carry a misplaced decimal point.

The van't Hoff factor \(i\) is the ratio of the colligative property of an electrolyte solution to the colligative property of a nonelectrolyte solution of the same concentration:

\(i = \dfrac{(\Delta T_f)}{(\Delta T_f)_0} = \dfrac{(\Delta T_b)}{(\Delta T_b)_0} = \dfrac{(\Delta P)}{(\Delta P)_0} = \dfrac{(\pi)}{(\pi)_0}\)

Equivalently it is the ratio of the actual number of moles of particles present in solution after dissociation to the number of moles of formula units dissolved, and also

\(i = \dfrac{\text{formula mass of substance}}{\text{observed molar mass of substance}}\)

It equals 1 for a nonelectrolyte, and ideally 2 for \(\mathrm{KNO_3}\) or NaCl and 3 for \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\) or \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\).

For an electrolyte \(\mathrm{A_xB_y}\) that gives \(n = x + y\) ions per formula unit and is dissociated to a degree \(\alpha\), one mole dissolved leaves \((1-\alpha)\) mol undissociated and produces \(x\alpha\) mol of cations and \(y\alpha\) mol of anions. The total moles of particles are

\((1-\alpha) + x\alpha + y\alpha = 1 + \alpha(n-1)\)

Since \(i\) is the actual moles of particles divided by the moles of formula units dissolved (which is 1),

\(i = 1 + \alpha(n - 1)\) or \(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}\)

So \(i\) rises linearly with the degree of ionization: \(i = 1\) when \(\alpha = 0\) (no ionization) and \(i = n\) when \(\alpha = 1\) (complete ionization).

The \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) solution has the higher freezing point depression, even though it is the more dilute of the two.

Freezing point depression is a colligative property, \(\Delta T_f = i K_f m\), so what matters is the number of particles, \(i \times m\), and not the formula concentration.

a. \(\mathrm{NaCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), so \(n = 2\) and \(i \times m = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

b. \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}} + 3\,\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\), so \(n = 5\) and \(i \times m = 5 \times 0.05 = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Taking \(K_f\) for water as 1.86 \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\), the depressions are 0.372 K for NaCl and 0.465 K for \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) — a factor of 1.25 in favour of \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\).

Raoult's law for a solution containing a nonvolatile solute states that the vapour pressure of the solvent over the solution is equal to the vapour pressure of the pure solvent multiplied by the mole fraction of the solvent in the solution. Thus

\(P_1 = P_1^0 x_1\)

where \(P_1\) is the vapour pressure of solvent above the solution, \(P_1^0\) that of the pure solvent and \(x_1\) the mole fraction of the solvent.

Because the solute is nonvolatile it contributes nothing to the vapour above the solution, so \(P_1\) is also the vapour pressure of the SOLUTION.

The boiling point of the water is LOWERED, not raised.

The boiling point elevation relation \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\) of section 2.8 is stated for a NONVOLATILE solute — one that contributes nothing to the vapour above the solution. Methyl alcohol is volatile, and more volatile than water (it boils at about 338 K against water's 373 K), so this solution is a solution of two volatile liquids and section 2.5 applies instead.

For two volatile components the total vapour pressure is

\(P = P_1^0x_1 + P_2^0x_2\)

At any given temperature \(P_2^0\) (methyl alcohol) is larger than \(P_1^0\) (water), so adding methyl alcohol RAISES the total vapour pressure above that of pure water. The mixture therefore reaches atmospheric pressure at a temperature BELOW \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\), and its boiling point is lower than that of pure water.

[Note: 1 mole of solute in 1 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of water is a 1 molal solution, so treating methyl alcohol as if it were nonvolatile would give \(\Delta T_b = K_b m = 0.512\ \mathrm{K} \times 1 = 0.512\ \mathrm{K}\) of elevation. That treatment is quoted here only to be set aside: its stated precondition, a nonvolatile solute, is not met.]

Osmotic pressure is the colligative property most often used for molecular mass determination.

The reason is that it is much LARGER than the other three colligative properties for the same solution, and is therefore measured far more precisely. A 0.001 M aqueous solution, for instance, depresses the freezing point by only about \(0.002^\circ\mathrm{C}\), which is barely measurable, while its osmotic pressure is of the order of a few tens of millimetres of mercury and is easily read.

Because of that sensitivity, only a small quantity of solute is needed, which makes the method especially useful for very expensive substances and for substances that can be prepared only in small quantities. The molar mass follows from

\(M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)
